reference.source: Fitzpatrick's Dermatology / Rook's Textbook of Dermatology
clinicalPearls: Presents as sudden, sharply bordered round or oval bald patches on otherwise normal-appearing scalp skin, without scarring or scale
Look for exclamation-mark hairs at the margins of active patches, where the shaft narrows towards the scalp
A positive hair-pull test at the periphery indicates ongoing disease activity
Extensive forms include loss of all scalp hair (totalis) and loss of all body hair (universalis); the ophiasis pattern along the occipital and temporal rim tends to respond poorly
Nail involvement such as fine regular pitting or roughening may accompany more severe or persistent disease
Associations with thyroid disease, vitiligo, atopy, and other autoimmune conditions warrant a focused history and examination
Regrowth often begins as fine depigmented or white hairs that later regain colour

Management ranges from watchful waiting in limited disease to intralesional or topical anti-inflammatory therapy, contact immunotherapy, and newer targeted systemic agents for extensive involvement; psychological impact should be addressed directly
reference.pathophysiology: Alopecia areata is an organ-specific autoimmune disorder in which the immune privilege of the hair follicle breaks down, allowing a T-cell-mediated attack focused on the anagen-phase follicular bulb. Interferon-gamma and other cytokines signalling through the JAK-STAT pathway drive a peribulbar lymphocytic infiltrate classically likened to a swarm of bees. Affected follicles prematurely enter catagen and telogen and produce dystrophic hairs, but the follicular stem-cell compartment is preserved, which is why regrowth remains possible even after long-standing loss. A polygenic predisposition interacts with environmental triggers, and there is overlap with other autoimmune diseases.
additionalDifferentials: Tinea capitis (scaly, inflamed, often with broken hairs and positive mycology)
Trichotillomania (irregular patches with hairs of varying length)
Telogen effluvium (diffuse shedding rather than discrete patches)
Traction alopecia at sites of chronic tension
Early scarring alopecias such as lichen planopilaris or discoid lupus
Secondary syphilis producing a moth-eaten pattern
additionalInvestigations: Usually a clinical diagnosis aided by dermoscopy showing exclamation-mark hairs, yellow dots, and black dots
Mycology (scrapings or culture) when tinea capitis cannot be excluded
Thyroid function and autoantibody testing when clinically indicated
Scalp biopsy reserved for atypical or diagnostically uncertain cases
Screening for associated autoimmune disease guided by symptoms
redFlags: Rapidly progressive or extensive loss suggesting evolution towards totalis or universalis
Scarring, scale, or follicular destruction indicating a different, potentially permanent alopecia
Significant psychological distress or impact on functioning requiring support
Diffuse hair loss with systemic symptoms prompting evaluation for an underlying disorder
reference.prognosis: Outcome is variable and unpredictable; limited single patches frequently regrow spontaneously within months, whereas early onset, extensive involvement, the ophiasis pattern, nail changes, and atopy predict a more prolonged and relapsing course.
pitfalls: Confusing non-scarring alopecia areata with a scarring alopecia and missing the window for treatment
Overlooking tinea capitis in children by not performing mycology
Attributing patchy loss to alopecia areata when hair-length variation points to trichotillomania
Underestimating the psychological burden and failing to offer support or counselling
management: Intralesional corticosteroids are first-line for limited patchy scalp disease, with potent topical corticosteroids as an alternative
Use topical minoxidil as an adjunct to promote regrowth
For extensive, rapidly progressive or totalis and universalis disease, consider oral JAK inhibitors such as baricitinib or ritlecitinib, which target the interferon-gamma driven JAK-STAT pathway
Consider topical immunotherapy such as diphencyprone for extensive or chronic patchy disease
Screen for and manage associated autoimmune conditions such as thyroid disease and vitiligo
Offer psychological support and camouflage options including wigs and cosmetic measures given the impact on wellbeing
Refer to dermatology for extensive, refractory or diagnostically uncertain disease
